payload.title: The Café Where Nothing Is for Sale
paragraphs: On the first Saturday of every month, a hall behind a library in Rotterdam fills with broken things. Visitors arrive carrying toasters, lamps, bicycle wheels and jackets with failed zips, and volunteers with screwdrivers sit waiting at long tables. Nothing is bought or sold. The idea, borrowed from a scheme started in the same city in 2009, has since spread to more than two thousand towns, and the tables now attract engineers, retired electricians and a steady supply of curious teenagers.

Organisers are quick to point out that the tonnage saved is modest. A hall might rescue forty kettles in a morning, which is nothing beside what a city throws away in an hour. The real product is confidence. Most visitors have never opened the case of an appliance and assume that what is inside is beyond them; they leave having watched a fuse or a frayed cable be replaced in ten minutes, and the next fault no longer sends them to a shop. Volunteers say the questions they are asked change noticeably after a second visit.

The obstacles are rarely technical. Manufacturers glue casings shut, sell spare parts only to approved dealers, and design circuit boards that cannot be opened without destroying them. Several European rules now require that common parts be available for a decade after a model is discontinued, but the fine print still allows firms to set the price. A repairer who can fix a machine in twenty minutes, and then finds the plastic clip costs more than a new machine, has met the limit of goodwill.

Volunteers at repair cafés have persuaded manufacturers to stop gluing their products shut and to give spare parts away.
The movement began in Rotterdam because the city had more retired electricians than anywhere else in Europe.

payload.title: Digging Up the Rivers We Buried
paragraphs: Almost every old city is built over water. As populations grew, the streams that once ran through them were treated as open drains, roofed with brick and finally paved over, and the roads that took their place still follow their bends. For a century this looked like straightforward progress: the smell was gone, and the land above was worth a fortune. Engineers assumed the pipes beneath would carry whatever the sky delivered.

That assumption has aged badly. A buried stream can only take the volume its Victorian builders imagined, and storms now arrive in shorter, heavier bursts. When the pipe fills, the water surfaces in basements. Seoul offered the most watched alternative when it removed an elevated motorway in 2003 and uncovered the Cheonggyecheon below, giving the flow room to spread. Summer temperatures beside the restored channel fell by several degrees, and the fish and herons that returned were photographed so often that other mayors began asking what it had cost.

The answer is that it costs a great deal, and not only in money. Uncovering a stream means taking road space away from drivers who have used it all their lives, and the land alongside becomes so desirable that the residents the scheme was meant to serve are often priced out. Cities that have done it well tend to have started small, with a single block of a minor tributary, and to have let the argument be settled by a summer of people sitting on the new banks rather than by a report.

questions.prompt: 本文の主旨として最も適切なものはどれですか。
options: Uncovering buried streams helps cities cope with heavier storms and cools them down, but it is expensive and politically difficult, so it works best when begun on a small scale.

Seoul's Cheonggyecheon project failed because the returning fish and herons attracted too many visitors to the area.
The main reason cities bury their rivers today is that riverside land has become too cheap to be worth keeping open.

options: Bringing a hidden river back to the surface solves real problems of flooding and heat, but its cost falls on drivers and poorer neighbours, so cautious, small beginnings are the surest route.
